raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient coronary support and drug delivery, then disappear, potentially restoring vasomotion, facilitating late expansive remodelling, reducing very-late stent-related events, and preserving future surgical or percutaneous options. The concept was attractive because permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES), although highly effective, leave a lifelong implant that may contribute to chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, impaired vasomotion, and difficulty with repeat intervention.

Early human experience began with polymeric poly-L-lactic acid scaffolds. The Igaki-Tamai device showed feasibility but required heat expansion and had bulky struts; long-term follow-up nevertheless supported the biological possibility of complete scaffold disappearance without a permanent metal cage [1,2]. Metallic resorption was also explored with the magnesium alloy AMS platform, which was safe but lost radial strength rapidly, leading to restenosis [3]. The first widely adopted drug-eluting BVS was the Absorb everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactic acid scaffold. Early ABSORB cohort studies demonstrated acceptable safety, late lumen enlargement, and signals of vasomotor recovery, reinforcing enthusiasm for the technology [4-9]. Other platforms, including the novolimus-eluting DESolve scaffold and the sirolimus-eluting magnesium DREAMS/Bioabsorbable Magmaris scaffold, attempted to improve radial strength, deliverability, and resorption kinetics [10,11].

Randomized evidence initially appeared reassuring. ABSORB II compared Absorb with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents and showed similar short-term clinical outcomes, although the scaffold did not meet its mechanistic coprimary endpoints of superior vasomotion or lumen gain [12]. ABSORB III, a pivotal randomized trial in relatively simple lesions, found non-inferiority for target-lesion failure at 1 year [13]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China similarly supported regulatory approval in selected patients [14,15]. In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, TROFI II suggested comparable 6-month healing by optical coherence tomography (OCT), while EVERBIO II extended randomized assessment into broader all-comer lesions [16,17]. These findings encouraged implantation outside strict trial criteria.

Subsequent longer follow-up changed the field. Meta-analyses and individual-patient datasets showed higher scaffold thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction with Absorb compared with contemporary metallic everolimus-eluting stents, particularly beyond 1 year [18]. Registry experience, including GHOST-EU, confirmed that real-world outcomes were less favourable than early trials, especially when scaffolds were used in small vessels, long lesions, calcified disease, bifurcations, or without meticulous implantation [19]. Mechanistic studies identified underexpansion, malapposition, edge dissection, strut discontinuity during resorption, and late intraluminal scaffold dismantling as contributors to thrombosis [20,21]. The AIDA trial, reflecting routine practice, reported a substantially higher rate of definite or probable device thrombosis with Absorb than with metallic DES [22]. Three-year ABSORB II results showed no late clinical advantage and an excess of adverse events [23]. Pooled analyses confirmed that excess risk clustered during the active bioresorption phase and was amplified in vessels smaller than recommended [24,25]. OCT registries of very-late scaffold thrombosis further emphasized late structural failure and uncovered struts as key mechanisms [26].

The procedural lesson from first-generation BVS was that implantation technique matters more than with metallic DES. Optimal practice evolved into “PSP”: aggressive lesion preparation, accurate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation with a non-compliant balloon. Intravascular imaging was strongly favoured because angiography underestimates vessel size and cannot reliably detect scaffold underexpansion or malapposition. ABSORB IV incorporated stricter vessel sizing and improved technique and showed better early outcomes than earlier experience, but it did not establish superiority over metallic DES [27]. Later patient-level analyses suggested that risk attenuated after complete resorption, but the early-to-midterm hazard offset the theoretical late benefit [28,29].

Current practice has therefore become conservative. First-generation Absorb was withdrawn from commercial use, and contemporary guidelines do not support routine BVS use in coronary intervention. Metallic second-generation DES remain the benchmark because they combine thin struts, excellent deliverability, low restenosis, and very low thrombosis rates. Nevertheless, the BVS concept has not been abandoned. Newer scaffolds aim for thinner struts, faster endothelialization, better radial strength, more predictable degradation, and improved visibility. Magnesium-based scaffolds are particularly attractive because they offer metallic mechanical behaviour with bioresorption, although robust randomized evidence against best-in-class DES is still limited [30].

In summary, BVS represent one of the most instructive translational experiences in interventional cardiology. The biological rationale remains compelling, but first-generation devices demonstrated that resorption alone is insufficient; safety depends on strut thickness, mechanical integrity, degradation kinetics, lesion selection, and implantation precision. Future scaffolds must prove not merely non-inferiority in simple lesions but a clinically meaningful advantage over excellent contemporary DES.
